architecture.name: Custom OCI 3-Tier Web App
architecture.description: OCI Flexible Load Balancer distributing traffic across 2× VM.Standard.E4.Flex-2OCPU VM instances backed by a single mysql-heatwave Database (us-ashburn-1).

components.notes: OCI Flexible Load Balancer base charge (us-ashburn-1). Bandwidth charged separately.
Flexible: 2 OCPU (4 AMD EPYC vCPUs), 16 GiB RAM. Comparable tier to AWS m5.large (us-ashburn-1).
MySQL HeatWave DB System: 2 OCPU, 16 GiB RAM (E4.Flex). OLTP + in-database analytics (us-ashburn-1).

scoreDriverNote: OCI uses its own latency, error, CPU, tail and throughput-shed coefficients fit to VM.Standard.E4.Flex 2-OCPU / MySQL HeatWave reference data, plus a +6.25 ms idle base-latency offset (EPYC + Flexible LB overhead) so idle P50 reproduces the documented floor. HeatWave's low in-memory error rates are captured by the fitted polynomial (Burst error matches closely), and a connection-pool goodput-shed term reproduces the documented Peak/Burst effective throughput (which sits below traffic × (1 − errorRate) due to admission back-pressure). The residual is in CPU: OCI's reference curve is unusually steep (low Normal 12 % yet high Burst 78 %), which the shared √-shaped compute curve plus the shared database CPU curve cannot fully track — leaving CPU slightly over-predicted at Normal and under-predicted at Peak/Burst.

referenceProvenance.costBasis: Fixed-fee public price-list comparison, not a measured bill: scored prediction uses itemized resource costs before display rounding and excludes modeled egress and load-balancer variable data processing/ALB LCUs. The load-balancer base hourly fee remains included; other resource charges are not removed.
referenceProvenance.note: Reference values are sourced from provider documentation and published load-test studies.

scenario.label: Idle
scenario.description: Minimal background traffic — keep-alive checks, health probes, and occasional real requests.

sources.citation: OCI VM.Standard.E4.Flex 2-OCPU (4 AMD EPYC vCPUs) + OCI Flexible LB: idle P50 ~18–22 ms, P95 ~42–50 ms. OCI Flexible LB adds ~4–6 ms more round-trip overhead than AWS ALB; EPYC vCPU scheduling latency is similar to x86 at idle. Source: OCI Load Balancer and Compute performance documentation.

OCI E4.Flex 2-OCPU at idle: ~3–5% CPU (OS + runtime on 4 EPYC vCPUs — lower relative utilisation than 1-OCPU due to more available cores). MySQL HeatWave (300 max connections) at 10 RPS: ~2 active connections; OCI network fabric transient errors ~0.12–0.18%. Source: OCI MySQL HeatWave documentation.
OCI Pricing (us-ashburn-1, August 2026): Flexible LB $0.0224/hr + 2× E4.Flex 2-OCPU ($0.074/hr each: 2 OCPU × $0.025 + 16 GB × $0.0015) + MySQL HeatWave $0.074/hr = $0.2444/hr.

scenario.label: Normal
scenario.description: Typical business-hours traffic with steady sustained load.

sources.citation: OCI E4.Flex 2-OCPU at ~50 RPS/instance: real-world P50 ~30–38 ms, P95 ~70–82 ms. The AWS-calibrated simulator under-predicts by ~20–25% because the latency formula does not model OCI's EPYC scheduling overhead or OCI LB network latency. With 4 vCPUs per instance, queuing at 50 RPS is minimal. Source: OCI Compute performance documentation.

OCI E4.Flex 2-OCPU (4 EPYC vCPUs) at ~50 RPS/instance: effective CPU ~10–14%. With 4 vCPUs handling 50 RPS, per-core utilisation is low; the AWS-calibrated sqrt-of-utilisation formula over-predicts because it was tuned to 2-vCPU m5.large scaling characteristics. Source: OCI Compute performance documentation.

MySQL HeatWave (300 max connections) at 100 RPS: ~20 concurrent connections = 6.7% pool utilisation. HeatWave in-memory query acceleration keeps connection hold times short; real-world error rate ~0.14–0.22%. Source: OCI MySQL HeatWave documentation.

scenario.label: Peak
scenario.description: Peak business load — product launch, end-of-day batch, or marketing campaign spike.

sources.citation: OCI E4.Flex 2-OCPU at ~250 RPS/instance: real-world P50 ~75–89 ms, P95 ~150–174 ms. The AWS-calibrated queuing-theory formula under-predicts OCI latency by ~20–25% at peak due to EPYC scheduling and OCI LB overhead. With 4 vCPUs at 250 RPS, the instance has meaningful headroom. Source: OCI performance best practices.

OCI E4.Flex 2-OCPU at 250 RPS/instance: real-world CPU ~44–52%. 4 EPYC vCPUs at 250 RPS load produce roughly half the per-core utilisation compared to a 2-vCPU AWS m5.large. Source: OCI Compute performance documentation.

MySQL HeatWave at 500 RPS: ~100 concurrent connections = 33% pool utilisation (300 max). HeatWave in-memory acceleration returns query results before connection hold time causes pool pressure; real-world error rate ~0.25–0.45%. Effective throughput ~487 RPS. Source: OCI MySQL HeatWave benchmarks.

scenario.label: Burst
scenario.description: Traffic burst exceeding normal peak — flash sale, viral event, or coordinated load test.

sources.citation: OCI E4.Flex 2-OCPU at ~500 RPS/instance: real-world P50 ~144–166 ms, P95 ~280–316 ms. OCI LB + EPYC scheduling overhead add ~15–20% vs the AWS-calibrated model at equivalent per-instance RPS. Source: OCI performance documentation.

OCI E4.Flex 2-OCPU at 500 RPS/instance: CPU ~74–82% as the 4 EPYC cores approach saturation under combined compute + network I/O load. Still below the saturation threshold a 2-vCPU instance would hit at the same RPS. Source: OCI Compute performance docs.

MySQL HeatWave at 1000 RPS: ~200 connections = 67% pool utilisation (300 max). HeatWave in-memory processing keeps connection hold times low; real-world error rate ~2.2–3.4% at 67% pool utilisation — lower than a disk-based DB at equivalent utilisation. Effective throughput ~882 RPS. Source: OCI MySQL HeatWave documentation.
